Al- though this study was prematurely unblinded, and all women were offered a 5-year course of tamoxifen, follow- up continued for 7 years and the incidence of breast cancer remained relatively constant for the 2 years after tamoxifen therapy was stopped.5 Preliminary results from 2 smaller randomised European studies did not confirm the benefit of tamoxifen in breast cancer prevention. The Italian study6 was in hysterectomised women with no par- ticular risk for breast cancer, and because of its size may not have been sufficiently powered to detect an effect of tamoxifen. The full follow-up7 of 5 years of treatment in this study found no difference in breast cancer incidence between tamoxifen and placebo groups. A subgroup anal- ysis of women at high risk of oestrogen-receptor positive breast cancer did find a protective effect from tamoxifen, and there was an apparent protective effect for women in this group who used HRT. However, this group was not identified at randomisation of the study and these results need to be confirmed. The British study8 of 8 years of tamoxifen or placebo was in women with a first-degree family history of breast cancer, and their median age was younger than in the US study. Although preliminary re- sults showed no benefit from tamoxifen, follow-up for a median of about 13 years did find a reduction in the risk of oestrogen-receptor positive tumours.9 This reduced risk also appeared to improve with longer follow-up. Initial re- sults of a further placebo-controlled study (IBIS-I)10 of women at increased risk of breast cancer found that during 5 years of tamoxifen use, the risk of all breast cancers was reduced by 32%. As in other studies, the reduction oc- curred in oestrogen-receptor positive tumours. Similar ad- verse effects were found with tamoxifen use, but there was also an unexpected increase in deaths from all causes in tamoxifen users. This may be associated with the excess in thromboembolic events reported, although statistical vari- ability could not be ruled out. Extended follow-up11 for a further median of 8 years found that the beneficial effect of tamoxifen was maintained, and that reduction in the risk of oestrogen-receptor positive tumours increased with longer follow-up. However, the rate of adverse effects of tamoxifen reduced after treatment stopped. A retrospec- tive analysis12 of the NSABP P-1 data for women who had developed invasive breast cancer found that in carriers of the oncogene BRCA2, but not BRCA1 carriers, there was a reduction in breast cancer similar to the reduction in oes- trogen-receptor positive cancer among all women in the study.
